reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: Caused most often by biallelic mutations in RAB23 (and less commonly MEGF8), inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern
Combines craniosynostosis (frequently multisuture, sometimes producing a cloverleaf skull) with both polydactyly and syndactyly of the hands and feet
Preaxial polydactyly of the feet with soft-tissue syndactyly is a useful distinguishing feature from the FGFR-related syndromes
Congenital heart disease is common and should be actively sought at diagnosis
Obesity, short stature, hypogenitalism in males and variable intellectual disability are recognised associations
The MEGF8-related form is often associated with laterality defects such as situs abnormalities
Because inheritance is recessive, recurrence risk for siblings is significant and warrants formal genetic counselling
Management is multidisciplinary, combining craniofacial vault surgery, cardiac care and limb reconstruction
reference.pathophysiology: Carpenter syndrome is a ciliopathy caused by loss of function of RAB23, a small GTPase that participates in vesicular trafficking and in the regulation of hedgehog signalling at the primary cilium. Disrupted hedgehog signalling during development perturbs cranial suture patterning, causing premature multisuture fusion, and disturbs limb patterning, producing the combination of polydactyly and syndactyly. The wide role of this pathway explains the associated cardiac, growth and genital anomalies; MEGF8 mutations affect a related pathway and add laterality defects.
additionalDifferentials: Apert syndrome (FGFR2, complex syndactyly without polydactyly)
Bardet-Biedl syndrome (ciliopathy with polydactyly and obesity)
additionalInvestigations: Molecular testing of RAB23 and MEGF8 to confirm the diagnosis
Three-dimensional cranial CT to characterise multisuture fusion
Echocardiography to detect congenital heart disease
Radiographs of the hands and feet to document polydactyly and syndactyly
MRI of the brain to assess structural anomalies and intracranial pressure concerns
Developmental assessment and, where MEGF8 is implicated, evaluation for laterality defects
redFlags: Unrecognised congenital heart disease causing haemodynamic compromise
Raised intracranial pressure from multisuture or cloverleaf skull fusion
Airway or feeding difficulty in the neonatal period
Laterality or situs anomalies in the MEGF8-related form
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends heavily on the severity of the craniosynostosis and any associated cardiac disease; with surgical correction and multidisciplinary support many children do well, though intellectual outcome is variable and some have significant learning difficulty.
pitfalls: Confusing it with an FGFR-related syndrome and missing the recessive inheritance and recurrence risk
Failing to screen for congenital heart disease at presentation
Overlooking the diagnostic clue of combined polydactyly and syndactyly
Not arranging developmental support because intellectual outcome varies
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
management: Staged surgical correction of the multisuture craniosynostosis, prioritising relief of raised intracranial pressure
Reconstructive hand and foot surgery to address the polydactyly and syndactyly
Active screening for and treatment of congenital heart disease at diagnosis
Assessment and management of associated features including obesity, short stature and male hypogenitalism
Evaluation for laterality and situs abnormalities where MEGF8 is implicated
Developmental and educational support tailored to the variable intellectual outcome
Multidisciplinary craniofacial, cardiac and clinical genetics care
Genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance, with molecular confirmation and family screening
